lesson.title: Meiosis I: Separating the Homologous Pairs
lesson.summary: Meiosis I is the reductional division of meiosis, in which homologous chromosome pairs, not sister chromatids, are separated into two haploid daughter cells.
lesson.body:
Meiosis I is the division that actually accomplishes what the rest of meiosis is named for: cutting the chromosome number in half by separating homologous chromosomes from each other. It begins with a diploid cell whose DNA has already been replicated, so each of the 46 human chromosomes, to use the human example, exists as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere.

Prophase I is the longest and most eventful phase of meiosis. Chromosomes condense, and, in a step with no equivalent in mitosis, each chromosome finds and pairs precisely with its homologous partner in a process called synapsis, forming a structure called a tetrad, since it contains four chromatids total, two from each homolog. While paired, non-sister chromatids from the two homologs exchange segments of DNA in a process called crossing over. The mechanics of synapsis and crossing over are detailed in the next chapter, but the essential point for now is that by the time prophase I ends, each homolog may carry a new mixture of maternal and paternal DNA, and the nuclear envelope has broken down as the spindle apparatus takes shape.

At metaphase I, it is entire tetrads, not individual chromosomes, that line up along the metaphase plate. Crucially, which homolog of each pair faces which spindle pole is random and independent of how every other pair is arranged, an effect called independent assortment. With 23 pairs in humans, this randomness alone generates millions of possible chromosome combinations in the resulting gametes, entirely apart from whatever variation crossing over adds.

Anaphase I is where meiosis I most clearly departs from mitosis. The two homologous chromosomes of each pair are pulled apart toward opposite poles, but, unlike in mitotic anaphase, the sister chromatids making up each homolog remain joined at their centromere and travel together as a single unit. What separates in anaphase I is homolog from homolog, not chromatid from chromatid.

By telophase I, two daughter cells have formed, each haploid in terms of chromosome number, one member of each original pair, but each of those chromosomes still consists of two sister chromatids. In many organisms cytokinesis follows immediately, and the cells move into meiosis II, covered next, without any further DNA replication in between.
